agent_notes: The packet's verse map puts the superscription (לְדָוִד) in 27:0 and the verse proper in 27:1; I kept the Hebrew verse as one unit and glossed לְדָוִד as 'of David / for David' (the lamed is ambiguous: author, dedication or collection).

Gloss 8 מָעוֹז: STEPBible 'refuge of'; I kept 'stronghold of' because the literal layer needs the fortress image Radak develops. The five English versions agree on 'strength' (KJV/ASV) or 'refuge'; the Hebrew word is a fortified place, not an abstract quality.

history.note: [consider] Drop the Shamash remark or mark it as background not drawn from the packet. (PS.27.1 Radak: "הצרה דומה לחשכה והתשועה ממנה היא האורה"; nothing on Shamash in the packet.)

agent_notes: כִּי with perfect עֲזָבוּנִי: KJV 'when ... forsake' treats it as a hypothetical; Ibn Ezra offers a future/perfect-of-certitude; Meiri says כי = 'when'. Rashi's comment on the begetting is a rabbinic homily (Lev. Rabbah) and not used in the dramatic layer. The literal layer keeps 'For my father and my mother have forsaken me'.

שׁוֹרְרָי: derived from שׁוּר 'to watch/ lie in wait' (Metzudat Zion links to Ps 56:3); STEPBible 'enemies' is a contextual gloss. YLT's 'my beholders' keeps the root sense. I glossed 'my watchers (foes)'.

וִיפֵחַ חָמָס: the form is a noun/participle 'one who breathes out violence' (Prov 6:19; 14:5, 'breathes out lies', sources not in the packet); Ibn Ezra reads it as a verb-like 'speaks violence', Rashi 'speakers of evil', Meiri 'speech'. STEPBible gloss 'and a witness of' is wrong lexically (it borrows the parallel with עֵד); I corrected it to 'and one breathing out'.

נֶפֶשׁ 'throat, appetite, will': Rashi, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion all gloss בְּנֶפֶשׁ as 'in the desire/will of'. Radak cites Gen 23:8. The Hebrew picture of a hungry throat links back to v. 2, 'to eat my flesh'.

The verse has no main clause: the Hebrew breaks off after 'unless I had believed…', and the apodosis (what would have happened) is left unsaid. KJV and ASV supply 'I had fainted' in italics, Webster in brackets; YLT and my literal layer leave the gap open. The dramatic layer lets the sentence trail off rather than supply a verb, which keeps the Hebrew's aposiopesis. Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra each fill it differently (the false witnesses would have destroyed me / I would have perished).

The word לולא carries extraordinary points (puncta extraordinaria) in the Masoretic text; the packet's form shows them as extra dots. I rely on Rashi and Radak, who both cite b. Berakhot 4a for the reason, and give no explanation of my own beyond that.

Corrected STEPBible gloss for token 3: 'to look' becomes 'to see (to experience)', since ראה with ב means to see something as an experience, not merely to look at it. Token 7 'living [people]' becomes 'the living'. 'Land of the living' is read as this life; the classical commentators split between this world (Metzudat David, Metzudat Zion) and the world to come (Radak, Meiri), which I note in the commentary without choosing.

Reviewer request addressed: the link between קוה and קַו 'line, cord' is removed from the note and the commentary; it is not in the packet's sources and I am not sure of it. Malbim is cited only for hope as an end in itself, Metzudat David only for the repetition as constancy. STEPBible glosses וְיַאֲמֵץ as 'so may it show strength'; I took it as a jussive of the hiphil of אמץ ('let it make strong' / 'may he make strong your heart', the subject being either the LORD or, by Ibn Ezra's reading, the LORD as agent). Ibn Ezra reads it transitive, so the LORD strengthens; the KJV 'he shall strengthen' follows that reading, and I kept it as a reading and not as the only possibility.

(PS.27.14 Malbim: "הקווי לה' היא תכלית לעצמה"; Metzudat David: "כפל הדבר להתמדתו" — no cord in either.)

agent_notes: מְרֵעִים 'evildoers' (hiphil participle of רעע); 'to eat my flesh' is read as the idiom of slander/devouring (cf. Job 19:22, Ps 14:4), but I did not cite it as a source since the packet does not supply it. Meiri and Radak take it as literal threat; Malbim splits the two motives.
לִי after אֹיְבַי is a dative of interest ('my enemies who were against me / to my cost'); STEPBible glosses it 'to me'. Translated 'mine' in the literal layer with the dative kept in the gloss.

תַּחֲנֶה (fem. verb) with מַחֲנֶה: Meiri notes מחנה as feminine here. Gloss 12 בְּזֹאת: Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David take it as 'in this [that I said: YHWH is my light]'; Ibn Ezra cites others who point forward to the one request of v. 4. I kept the neutral 'in this'.

לְבַקֵּר: commentators split between 'inquire' (Ibn Ezra via Lev 27:33, Metzudat Zion, KJV), 'visit each morning' (Rashi's Dunash, Ibn Ezra's 'others') and 'contemplate'. I chose 'to inquire' for the literal layer and mention 'morning' in the commentary; the sound play with בֹּקֶר is real but not certain.
Gloss 7 שִׁבְתִּי is an infinitive construct with 1cs suffix ('my dwelling'), not a finite verb; STEPBible's 'to dwell I' is awkward. Glossed 'my dwelling'.

Reviewer request addressed: the Targum remark now says what it says (it renders 'in his booth' as 'in his shade/shelter', בְּטַלְלֵיהּ, and keeps a verb of hiding) and no longer claims a treasure sense. The treasure sense of צפן is my own reading and is stated on its own, with no source. Verse 5 is the only one in the window where the five English versions split on סֻכֹּה: 'pavilion' (KJV, ASV, Webster), 'tabernacle' (YLT), 'tent' (BBE). I kept 'booth' in the literal layer, 'shelter' in the dramatic one. The form is a spelling of סֻכּוֹ 'his booth' (STEPBible lemma סֹךְ, 'covert'); both nouns are from the root סכך 'cover'. Rashi (Seder Olam Rabbah) and Ibn Ezra take it as the temple or Jerusalem; I report both as readings.

Rashi: sacrifices over which a song is said; Ibn Ezra: of rejoicing; Malbim: thanksgiving for victory with the same word used for war-trumpets (Num 10:9). I kept 'a shout' in the literal layer and the dual (joy / war-cry) sense in the commentary.

agent_notes: אֶקְרָא as a relative-like clause 'I call'. Ibn Ezra supplies אשר ('[when] I call'); KJV/ASV 'when I cry'. Literal layer keeps the bare asyndeton.

Reviewer request addressed: the sentence saying the KJV collapses the repeated פָּנִים into a single 'face' is deleted. The commentary now notes only the echo 'my face ... your face' in the Hebrew. The one thing I do say about the KJV is that 'When thou saidst' supplies a temporal clause and a speaker (God) that the Hebrew does not have; YLT keeps the heart as the speaker, BBE, ASV and Webster follow the KJV. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak (quoting the editor's note), Meiri and Metzudat David give four different readings of לְךָ; I give the main two and choose the plain one: the heart speaks, quoting what it hears as God's call.

agent_notes: KJV 'Hide not thy face far from me' adds 'far' (not in the Hebrew); 'put not thy servant away' for תַּט־בְּאַף is a paraphrase. Rashi (as 'incline/bow, cf. Ps 18:10') and Ibn Ezra (transitive: do not cause your servant to lean/fall) read 'turn aside' as transitive. I translated 'do not turn [your servant] aside in anger'.
